text: Shoot photos in daylight near a window. Natural light sells more than any filter.
Use a plain background: a white wall, a wooden floor or a neutral bedsheet.
Take 5 to 8 photos: front, back, label, size tag, any flaw and one worn or styled shot.
Photograph every flaw up close. Buyers who see it first rarely open a dispute.
Iron or steam clothes before shooting. Wrinkles read as worn out.
Keep the first photo a clean square crop. It is the only image shown in the feed.
Title formula: Brand + item type + colour + size + one key detail (material, model, year).
Write the size exactly as the label says and add the EU size if it differs.
Put the brand name first in the title. Most buyers search by brand.
Mention 'new with tags' or 'never worn' in the title when it is true.
Avoid all caps and emoji walls in titles. They look like spam and hurt search.
Check sold listings, not active ones, to see what an item really goes for.
Price about 10 percent above your floor so you can accept the first fair offer.
Drop the price of a stale listing by a small step every week instead of one big cut.
Turn on offers. Many buyers only buy when they feel they negotiated.
Round prices like 15 look cheaper to scan than 14.99 on mobile.
Offer bundle discounts. One parcel with three items costs you one trip to the post.
Group matching items (same size, same brand) so bundles form naturally.
When someone likes several items, message a bundle price before they move on.
Weigh and measure items before listing so the shipping option is right the first time.
Keep a stock of poly mailers, tape and tissue so you can ship the same day.
Ship within 24 hours. Fast shipping lifts reviews, and reviews lift sales.
Reuse clean boxes and mailers. Buyers care about the item, not fresh packaging.
Print the label at home or use a parcel locker to skip the queue at the post office.
Fold clothes neatly and add a short thank-you note. Repeat buyers come from small touches.
For local pickups meet in a busy public place in daylight, never at your home.
Accept only the platform's payment or cash in hand. Never send items before payment clears.
Keep all messages inside the app. Off-platform chat removes buyer and seller protection.
Be wary of buyers who overpay and ask for a refund of the difference. That is a classic scam.
Film yourself packing high-value items. Video settles most 'item not as described' claims.
List a few items every day instead of twenty at once. Fresh listings get more views.
Relist or refresh items that have had no views in two weeks.
Answer questions within an hour when you can. Slow replies lose impatient buyers.
Describe fabric, fit and measurements. Fewer questions means faster sales.
Note where the item was bought and how often it was worn. Honest history builds trust.
Seasonal timing matters: list coats in September and swimwear in April.
Sell in Latvian and English. A two-language description reaches both local and EU buyers.
Check cross-border shipping options for Lithuania and Estonia. Baltic buyers often pay more.
Source stock at second-hand kilo shops and end-of-season sales, then list within a week.
Keep a simple spreadsheet: buy price, sale price, fees, shipping. Profit per item, not revenue, decides what to source next.
Commit small, commit often. A ten-line commit is easy to review and easy to revert.
Write the test for the bug before you fix it. The fix then proves itself.
Name things for what they do, not how they do it. A reader should not need the body.
Delete dead code instead of commenting it out. Git keeps the history for you.
Read the error message twice before searching. Most of the answer is in it.
Pin dependency versions in requirements.txt so builds stay reproducible.
Put configuration at the top of the file or in one config object. Nobody hunts for magic numbers.
Use a virtual environment per project. System Python is for the system.
Log inputs and outputs at boundaries: network calls, file writes, external commands.
When an AI coding agent suggests a change, read the diff before you accept it.
Give coding agents one task per prompt and a way to verify it, like a test or a command.
Keep a CLAUDE.md or README in the repo root. Agents and humans both read it first.
Automate the task you did by hand three times. Once is not a pattern.
Make scripts idempotent: running twice should not create duplicates or double-send.
Add a dry-run flag to every script that writes, sends or deletes.
Schedule jobs at odd minutes like :17. Everyone else runs at :00 and queues up.
Store secrets in environment variables or repo secrets, never in code or commits.
Every automated job should write one line of output that says what it did.
In n8n or similar tools, add an error branch that sends you a message. Silent failures cost the most.
Keep raw data and processed data in separate folders so you can rebuild from scratch.
Back up the one file your automation depends on. Everything else can be regenerated.
